What this number is, and what it is not

Carbon intensity is the average grams of CO2 released per kilowatt-hour of electricity on the GB grid this half hour. It is an average across the whole system, not a property of your supply: buying a green tariff does not change the physics of what is running, and neither does living next to a wind farm. What it measures is how clean the country’s electricity is at this moment.

⚠ Half the time, the current figure is a forecast. The settled actual for a half hour does not exist until after that half hour has finished and been reconciled, so a dashboard showing you “now” is showing a prediction. This page labels which one you are looking at, every time, because a forecast presented as a measurement is the most common error in this whole subject.

⚠ The bands move, and almost nothing says so

NESO redraws the boundaries between “low”, “moderate” and “high” as the grid decarbonises. A reading that earned “low” a few years ago earns “moderate” today without a single gram having changed. The scale above is the current year’s.

The practical consequence: comparing band labels across years compares two different rulers. If you want to know whether the grid got cleaner, compare the grams. The label tells you how today’s reading stands against today’s expectations, which is a useful but different question.

Why the fuel mix and the carbon do not line up

The two strips in the panel above are the same fuels measured twice — once as a share of the electricity, once as a share of the emissions — and they are deliberately drawn to the same scale so the mismatch is visible. Gas is routinely under a third of the generation and most of the carbon. Nuclear and wind are the reverse.

This is why “renewables hit a record share” and “carbon intensity was unremarkable” can both be true of the same day: what decides the intensity is not how much clean generation ran, it is how much gas had to run alongside it.
